hints: Think about what type of gas test you expect when a carbonate meets any dilute acid.
Recall the thermal decomposition of a Group 2 nitrate gives a solid oxide plus two gases, and one of them is brown.
Compare an oxide reacting with acid, which just makes salt and water with no fizz, to a carbonate reacting with acid, which fizzes, and check if Group 2 oxides can act as acids too.
walkthrough:
**Test the carbonate with acid**

All metal carbonates react with dilute acids to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. That gas is seen as bubbles or effervescence.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{MCO}_3 + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{M(NO}_3)_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check the nitrate on heating**

Group 2 nitrates do not give nitrogen gas. They decompose to the metal oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen.

Chemical equation:
$$2\text{M(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Check the oxide with acid and its acid-base character**

Group 2 oxides are basic oxides. With dilute $\text{HCl}$ they neutralise to form a salt and water only, so no bubbles form.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{MO} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
They are not amphoteric because they do not react with bases, only with acids. Only the carbonate plus acid statement fits all the facts.

options.A: Correct. Group 2 carbonates, from $\text{MgCO}_3$ to $\text{BaCO}_3$, all react with dilute nitric acid to release $\text{CO}_2$ gas, seen as bubbles. This is the standard carbonate test.
options.B: Incorrect. Heating gives the oxide, nitrogen dioxide ($\text{NO}_2$) and oxygen, not nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$). Students often confuse $\text{NO}_2$ with $\text{N}_2$ because both contain nitrogen.
options.C: Incorrect. Oxides neutralise acids to give salt plus water only, with no gas evolved, so no bubbles. The fizzing with acid is characteristic of carbonates, not oxides.
options.D: Incorrect. Group 2 oxides are basic, not amphoteric. They react with acids but do not react with alkalis. Amphoteric behaviour is seen for $\text{BeO}$ and aluminium oxide, not for Mg to Ba oxides.
